lead: No two cubes from the same concrete break at the same load, and no two days put the same load on a floor. Limit state design therefore does not start from a single "strength" or "load" but from a cautious value at the unsafe end of each scatter: the characteristic strength near the weak end of the test results, and the characteristic load near the heavy end of the loads. Partial safety factors are applied to these values later. This chapter shows how the characteristic values are found from a mean and a standard deviation, and how the same rule is used backwards to set the target strength of a concrete mix.
prereq: You need: the idea of a limit state from limit state philosophy, and mean and standard deviation from statistics.

sections.h3: Characteristic strength: the lower 5 % of the results

blocks.text: IS 456 defines the characteristic strength of a material as the strength below which not more than 5 % of the test results are expected to fall. For concrete it is fck, the 28-day strength of 150 mm cubes; grade M25 means fck = 25 N/mm². For steel it is fy, the yield or 0.2 % proof stress; Fe415 means fy = 415 N/mm².

Test results from one mix cluster around their mean μ, the average. The standard deviation σ measures how widely they spread: a well-controlled site has a small σ. Cube strengths follow a normal (bell-shaped) distribution closely, and for a normal distribution 5 % of the values lie more than 1.645σ below the mean. IS 456 rounds 1.645 to 1.65:

blocks.where: μ is the mean cube strength and σ the standard deviation, both in N/mm².

blocks.text: Why not use the mean? Half of all the concrete would then be weaker than the value assumed in design. Using the 5 % value means only about one cube in twenty is weaker, and the partial safety factor covers that remaining risk. The same mean with a larger σ gives a lower f<sub>ck</sub>, so good quality control is rewarded with a higher grade.

sections.h3: Target mean strength for a mix

blocks.text: A mix designer works the rule backwards. To be sure that a mix will be at least M25, it must be proportioned for a target mean strength above 25 N/mm²:

blocks.where: s is the standard deviation expected on that site. When no site data exist, IS 456 gives assumed values: 3.5 N/mm² for M10 and M15, 4.0 N/mm² for M20 and M25, and 5.0 N/mm² for M30 to M50 (Table 8, for good site control).

blocks.text: For M25 the target is 25 + 1.65 × 4 = 31.6 N/mm²; for M30 it is 30 + 1.65 × 5 = 38.25 N/mm². The mix is designed for the target, so that its weakest 5 % still reaches the grade.

For loads the unsafe direction is upward. IS 456 defines the characteristic load as the load that has a 95 % probability of not being exceeded during the life of the structure. If a load is described by a mean μQ and a standard deviation σQ,

blocks.where: Q<sub>k</sub> is the characteristic load; μ<sub>Q</sub> and σ<sub>Q</sub> are in the same unit, kN or kN/m².

blocks.text: Enough statistics rarely exist for real loads, so IS 456 takes the loads of IS 875 (dead, imposed, wind, snow) and IS 1893 (earthquake) as the characteristic loads. Dead load, worked out from sizes and densities, has little scatter; imposed load, from people and goods, has much more; wind and earthquake loads are set for a chosen return period.
Characteristic values describe the material or the load; they carry no extra safety. The design values come from them through the partial safety factors.

examples.question: Thirty cube tests at 28 days on the concrete of a building site give a mean strength of 32 N/mm² and a standard deviation of 4 N/mm². Find the characteristic strength and the grade the concrete may be called.
steps: Mean μ = 32 N/mm²; standard deviation σ = 4 N/mm².
The grades are steps of 5 N/mm². Since 25.4 ≥ 25 but < 30, the concrete may be called M25.
Check the meaning: about 5 % of the cubes, 1 or 2 of 30, are expected below 25.4 N/mm².
examples.answer: f<sub>ck</sub> = 25.4 N/mm², so the concrete is M25 (not M30).

examples.question: A contractor must supply M25 concrete. (a) With no site data, what target mean strength should the mix be designed for? (b) After a few months the site standard deviation is found to be 3 N/mm². What target is needed now? (c) A floor's imposed load is modelled with a mean of 2.4 kN/m² and a standard deviation of 0.6 kN/m². Find its characteristic value.
steps: Assumed standard deviation for M25 (IS 456 Table 8): s = 4.0 N/mm².
With s = 3 N/mm²: target = 25 + 1.65 × 3 = 25 + 4.95 = 29.95 N/mm², about 30.0 N/mm². Better control lets the site use a leaner, cheaper mix.

traps: f<sub>ck</sub> is the 5 % value, not the mean. A mix with a mean of 32 N/mm² is M25, not M30.
Strengths use the minus sign, μ − 1.65σ; loads use the plus sign, μ + 1.65σ. A high load and a low strength are the unsafe cases.
The target mean strength is f<sub>ck</sub> + 1.65s, above the grade. Designing a mix for a mean of exactly 25 N/mm² gives an f<sub>ck</sub> of about 25 − 6.6 = 18.4 N/mm² when s = 4.
Characteristic values carry no factor of safety; the design values are 0.67f<sub>ck</sub>/γm, f<sub>y</sub>/γm and γ<sub>f</sub> Q<sub>k</sub>.
Round a calculated f<sub>ck</sub> down to a grade: 25.4 N/mm² is M25, never M30.

quiz.q: Define characteristic strength as in IS 456.
quiz.a: The strength of the material below which not more than 5 % of the test results are expected to fall.

quiz.q: Define characteristic load as in IS 456.
quiz.a: The load that has a 95 % probability of not being exceeded during the life of the structure.

quiz.q: Why is the mean cube strength not used as f<sub>ck</sub>?
quiz.a: Half of the concrete would be weaker than the design value. The 5 % value is cautious enough that the partial safety factor can cover the rest.

quiz.q: Why does the same mean strength give a lower f<sub>ck</sub> on a badly controlled site?
quiz.a: Poor control means a larger standard deviation, and f<sub>ck</sub> = μ − 1.65σ falls as σ grows.

quiz.q: Cube results have a mean of 40 N/mm² and a standard deviation of 5 N/mm². Find f<sub>ck</sub> and the grade.
Find the target mean strength for M30 with the IS 456 assumed standard deviation.
Mix A has a mean of 35 N/mm² and σ = 3 N/mm²; mix B the same mean and σ = 6 N/mm². Which gives the higher grade?
quiz.a: A: 35 − 4.95 = 30.05 N/mm², M30. B: 35 − 9.9 = 25.1 N/mm², M25. The steadier mix earns a higher grade at the same mean.

quiz.q: A student writes Q<sub>k</sub> = μ<sub>Q</sub> − 1.65σ<sub>Q</sub>. Correct the statement.
quiz.a: For a load the unsafe case is a high value, so Q<sub>k</sub> is the upper 5 % fractile: Q<sub>k</sub> = μ<sub>Q</sub> + 1.65σ<sub>Q</sub>. The minus sign belongs to strengths.

beyond: IS 456 also gives acceptance rules for cube results on site (each group of samples and each single result must reach set margins over f<sub>ck</sub>), and IS 10262 sets out mix design with the target strength. Full reliability analysis replaces the single 1.65 with probability models for every load and strength and a target reliability index. Search next for "IS 456 acceptance criteria for concrete", "IS 10262 mix design" and "structural reliability index".

figure.caption: Cube results of the worked example spread about their mean of 32 N/mm² with a standard deviation of 4 N/mm². The shaded tail holds the weakest 5 %; its edge, 1.65σ below the mean, is the characteristic strength 25.4 N/mm², so the concrete is called M25.

spec.aria: Bell curve of cube strength from 16 to 48 N/mm², peaking at the mean of 32. A shaded left tail of 5 % ends at 25.4 N/mm², marked fck, which is 6.6 N/mm² (1.65 sigma) below the mean.
